The post Once globally preeminent, U.S. universities are sliding into decline appeared first on The Hechinger Report.
full_text:
The nation was distracted by other things when a quiet warning sounded: Support was diminishing for American academic research that had led to breakthroughs and innovation.

That familiar-sounding worry came not this year, but near the end of World War II, in a pivotal government study by the wartime Office of Scientific Research and Development.

The response then: infusions of government cash that would propel the U.S. higher education system into international preeminence over the subsequent decades.

American colleges and universities rose to the ranks of the best in the world. They attracted top scholars who won a disproportionate number of Nobel Prizes. They helped drive the innovation economy. As trade deficits beset other industries, education became the sixth-largest U.S. services export. At their peak enrollment, international students brought in more than $40 billion a year.

Now, as a new academic year begins, American dominance in higher education globally is incontrovertibly in decline, according to data, international rankings and independent experts.

The slide has been accelerated by a year and a half of funding cuts, restrictions on international students and curbs on what can be said or taught. But it began before those political challenges, with enrollment declines, lackluster returns on ever-rising prices and public mistrust.

“It takes a while for all of these problems to trickle down, but they are beginning to trickle down,” said Eric Mlyn, a faculty fellow at the Kenan Institute for Ethics at Duke University who studies academic freedom.

Related: Interested in innovations in higher education? Subscribe to our free biweekly higher education newsletter.

Top scholars are leaving. Fewer international students are coming. U.S. universities are slipping in international rankings. And American universities have failed to keep pace as other countries pour resources into their higher education systems.

Chinese institutions, for example, have increased their production of graduates with doctoral degrees much faster than American ones in the critical fields of science, technology, engineering and math. Rather than expanding, U.S. doctoral programs are now admitting fewer candidates or have stopped accepting new applicants altogether.

This has myriad impacts on all Americans. Falling behind in research imperils the nation’s economic competitiveness, for instance. And attracting fewer international learners — and the subsidies they represent to universities’ bottom lines — is already affecting the services and majors available to domestic students, and could increase the cost.

So dire has the situation become that the American Academy of Arts and Sciences hosted a discussion about it in June. The title: “Is the U.S. Losing Its Edge as a Global Education Leader?”

The answer is yes, said Mlyn, who was one of the panelists. “There are so many issues threatening America’s global standing,” he said.

The number of U.S. universities in the top 100 of the QS World University Rankings has fallen from 31 to 26 in the past 10 years, while Chinese universities are moving up. The Times Higher Education World University Rankings still puts seven U.S. universities among the top 10. But the smallest number ever made the top 500, while Asian universities rose.

Related: As international enrollment falls, U.S. students face program cuts and higher prices

International standings like these “are the global symbol for geopolitical strength on the world stage, and they’re very influential in people’s decision about where to study,” said Phil Baty, the Times Higher’s chief global affairs officer. “If you start seeing the slow diminution of rankings, that means you’re becoming less attractive to that talent. Then it could be a really serious downward spiral.”

In the next Times Higher rankings — due out Sept. 30 — U.S. institutions continue to fall in comparative measures of reputation and research quality, Baty said.

“It does feel like a tipping point,” he said.

Universities in China annually turn out nearly 50 percent more Ph.D. graduates in science, technology, engineering and math than U.S. universities do, according to the National Science Foundation, or NSF. That’s partly a reflection of China’s larger population. But the pace of STEM Ph.D. production is also rising much more quickly in China than in the United States. It doubled in the 15 years ending in 2022, while the number of U.S. Ph.D. graduates in STEM rose two-fifths as fast, or by 41 percent, an analysis by fDi Intelligence found.

Chinese universities now hold seven of the top 10 places in the Leiden Rankings from the Centre for Science and Technology Studies at Leiden University, which ranks institutions based on the number of journal articles published by their faculties — a seemingly arcane but consequential measure of academic productivity in which Harvard has fallen from first in the world to third.

Researchers in China produced 28 percent of English language articles about artificial intelligence, worldwide, between 2018 and 2023, compared with 16 percent by scholars in the United States, according to the Emerging Technology Observatory at Georgetown University.

While they may have produced less research during that period than their Chinese counterparts, American scholars still ranked higher on how often their work was cited by others, the NSF noted — an important indication of its relative quality. And some of the most prestigious U.S. universities were still holding their own at the top of those most recent international rankings.

Related: Threats of more closings have colleges and students worrying about how to save themselves

But the Trump administration has since cut billions of dollars in research funding, resulting in layoffs and uncertainty. And while many of those initial cuts were restored by courts, federal agencies have slowed the awarding of new grants.

The administration’s 2027 budget request would reduce spending on the NSF and National Institutes of Health by 55 percent and 13 percent, respectively, according to the nonpartisan law and policy organization the Brennan Center for Justice, and shift some of what money remains away from universities.

“We have the success of the postwar period to show that the current model works pretty well,” said Steven Durlauf, an economist at the University of Chicago’s Harris School of Public Policy, referring to the historic role of the federal government in supporting academic research. Today, with funding uncertainty at least and cuts at worst, said Durlauf, “we’re on a suicidal trajectory.”

Related: More than a quarter of private colleges are at risk of closing, new projection shows

Blaming the interruptions in funding that have already occurred, top research universities have admitted 15 percent fewer doctoral students for the coming fall, including in fields such as artificial intelligence and quantum computing, according to the Association of American Universities, or AAU. Many didn’t take any new doctoral students at all.

Doctoral programs train scientists to teach and conduct research in fields including technology and treatments for medical problems.

“America faces the alarming prospect of losing an entire generation of scientific talent,” the AAU says.

Just after the start of the second Trump administration, about half of Ph.D. students and postdoctoral researchers in bioengineering said they were likely to leave academia, according to a survey by researchers at Harvard, MIT and elsewhere. The proportion who said they’d likely leave the United States was also up.

Three in four U.S.-based researchers overall have considered leaving the country, according to another survey, by the journal Nature, conducted before some of the Trump administration’s harshest actions against universities and colleges.

Forty-five percent of faculty in yet another survey, by researchers at the Harvard Graduate School of Education, said they had considered jobs outside of higher education in the last three years, and a third that they had considered opportunities outside of the United States. Most said changes in state or federal policy were instrumental in their job searches.

At least 85 scholars have moved to China since the start of 2024, CNN reporting found, including several at the top of their fields — most recently, Nobel Prize-winning chemist Omar Yaghi, who is leaving the University of California, Berkeley, for Tsinghua University in China to help establish an institute that will use AI to speed up the development of new materials.

American scientists collectively submitted 32 percent more applications for jobs abroad in the first quarter of last year than in the same period the year before, according to a separate analysis by Nature.

U.S. universities “have been magnets for talent because they have provided an exchange: ‘Come build your research lab at our university — you’ll get all these talented students, we have labs, we have government funding,’ ” said Kumar Garg, a science and technology adviser in the Obama administration and now president of Renaissance Philanthropy, which helps channel private funds to research. “If that bundle starts unraveling, this no longer works.”

Meanwhile, the flow of international students coming to the United States has slowed dramatically, with as much as a 22 percent decline in the number who arrived last summer compared with the summer before.

Nearly six in 10 universities and colleges say the number of applications they received from international students fell again for the academic year about to start, a survey by the Institute of International Education found. More than 40 percent reported a “substantial” decline in applications for graduate study. NAFSA: Association of International Educators and the education technology company JB International project a drop of 111,000 international students this fall, costing the economy $3.4 billion.

“The U.S. has thrived because the world’s smartest people flock to the United States, and that is definitely stalling,” said Baty, of the Times Higher.

This slide follows federal delays in issuing new student visas, the detentions and deportations of international students for their political activism and screenings of international student applicants’ social media posts.

Even before those steps, however — as the price of U.S. higher education continued to rise — “cost was a larger reason” for international students reconsidering coming to the United States, said Rona Aydin, who works with them as founder of the international college admissions counseling company Oriel Admissions.

Now, said Aydin, prospective applicants who previously would have only considered American universities “are also thinking about backup countries. That’s a shift.”

Yet another rule, restricting international students to four years in the United States, takes effect Sept. 15. Four years is less time than is needed to complete many Ph.D. and other academic programs, and the new limit is likely to further reduce the supply of international students coming to the country.

Related: Facing political attack and falling enrollment, colleges take the fight to … each other

Also, while it’s still too early to see their effects, new limits on federal loans for graduate study will leave about one-fourth of domestic graduate-school borrowers unable to continue to pay for their educations, projections suggest.

In some states, faculty have faced constraints on what they can teach and threats to protections such as tenure.

Institutional autonomy at U.S. universities has eroded by 50 percent in the decade ending in 2025, and especially since the first Trump administration, according to the Academic Freedom Index produced by researchers at Germany’s University of Erlangen-Nuremberg.

“The decline in institutional autonomy in the United States stands out as a case of fast and steep deterioration,” the researchers wrote in March.

Tenure can keep scientists from leaving academia for better-paying jobs in private industry, as more may now do, said Kenan Sahin, author of “American Educational Excellence,” a book about the strengths of the U.S. education system, and a life member of the governing board at MIT, which he attended as an international student before founding what would become a multibillion-dollar tech company.

Those researchers without tenure who remain at universities may stick to “safe” ideas rather than seek out potential breakthroughs and risk failure, Sahin said.

Seventy percent of Americans now say higher education in the United States is going in the wrong direction, up from 56 percent in 2020, according to Pew. Adults who went to college are more likely to say this than those who didn’t.

That falloff in confidence began before the current political attacks and is largely because of people’s skepticism about what they’re getting for their money, Pew’s and other surveys show.

The United States spends among the most in the world on higher education, according to the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development, or OECD. But it ranks 15th and 17th, respectively, in the proportion of 25- to 34-year-olds who have degrees, depending on whether their parents did or didn’t go to college. That’s down from second overall 20 years ago.

Related: As college graduates fret over finding jobs, a record shortage of workers is projected

The impact of these many intersecting trends is already underway.

There have been more than 320 instances of college and university layoffs, program cuts, department eliminations and closings since January 2024, according to the database CollegeCuts, which tracks this. Even Harvard’s Faculty of Arts and Sciences is running a $350 million deficit, which it attributes partly to an increased federal tax on its endowment.

“Universities went through a multidecade period where they existed in a bipartisan halo, where people might disagree about lots of things, but having cutting-edge universities was a thing everybody could agree on and was willing to invest in,” Garg said.

U.S. higher education institutions “really are deep wells of talent. Their strengths are real,” he said. But “we should not sleep on the fact that if we don’t adapt and navigate this moment, we’re going to wake up and all of the premier universities won’t be in the United States, and we’ll wonder how that happened.”

The post OPINION: Why investing in rural education can bolster local economies and help students build a future close to home appeared first on The Hechinger Report.
full_text:
Morgan County, Tennessee, is a rural community shaped by strong relationships, deep attachment to place and a shared commitment to its future. Its public lands and tourism economy are part of that story, as are the intergenerational ties, civic commitment and local institutions that hold the community together.

Like many rural areas, Morgan County also faces real economic challenges: More than half of its population struggles to afford basic household necessities, and 15 percent of its residents live below the poverty line.

That’s why the efforts of Roane State Community College to reshape what student success means are so important. Helping individual students earn credentials is not enough: The school also aims to strengthen the long-term economic vitality of the entire region.

In many areas, community colleges are the main driver of economic mobility. By expanding access to postsecondary education, creating clearer pathways into sustainable local careers and working alongside employers, schools and community organizations, they help ensure that residents can build stable futures close to home. They need more support.

Related: Interested in innovations in higher education? Subscribe to our free biweekly higher education newsletter.

Rural higher education has never been a high national priority, even though these institutions are not only educators but also employers, workforce hubs and cultural centers. Now, America’s roughly 1,000 rural colleges and regional universities are facing distinct challenges, including declining enrollment and, among their students, persistent poverty, long travel distances, limited choice in local industries and uneven broadband access that restricts educational opportunities.

Economic pressures are already shaping what institutions can offer, causing reductions in programs and constraints on capacity.

At the same time, these schools must stretch every dollar to address not only the academic needs of their students but also their basic needs: food and housing security, child care, transportation and more; there is a great need to learn and share what is working to help these schools achieve their missions.

Successful rural community colleges are building pathways to help students find work that leads to sustainable careers at a time of significant economic change. They are redesigning programs to align with emerging industries, from advanced manufacturing to information technology. They are partnering with business and community organizations to identify opportunities for future local jobs and are reaching beyond their walls to support out-of-school learners. They are creating dual-enrollment opportunities for high school students and are supporting adult learners looking for sustainable careers close to home.

Roane State embodies this approach by working in partnership with mayors, school leaders, local companies and community groups to bolster the economic prospects of the entire region, from emerging industry and digital jobs to health care and computer technology.

Elsewhere, rural colleges are taking similar initiatives: At Louisiana State University at Eunice, digital skills badges and a health care partnership are linking coursework to local careers. Columbia-Greene Community College in New York offers stronger student supports and microcredentials tied to labor market demand. Southeast Kentucky Community and Technical College has expanded training through partnerships with workforce agencies and community organizations.

Although rural students complete high school at a higher rate than the national average, reports show that only 29 percent of young adults (18- to 24-year-olds) in rural areas enroll in college compared to 42 percent of those in suburban areas and 48 percent in urban areas. Research also shows a 12-percentage-point gap between bachelor’s degree attainment in rural areas and urban communities.

At the same time, rural employers struggle to fill critical roles in teaching, health care and other skilled fields like accounting. Many rural communities lose college-educated residents to larger cities, making long-term economic development more difficult.

Related: OPINION: Rural community colleges are uniquely positioned to tackle complex regional challenges and drive community transformation. Here’s how

And yet there is little evidence about what strategies are most effective in supporting institutions as they attempt to meet the challenges of declining enrollment, slowing population growth, workforce needs and persistent poverty, and no readily accessible national data source that reports annual college attendance or completion rates among rural high school students by state.

Ultimately, we don’t know which homegrown innovations are making a difference for rural students. Too often, policymakers leave rural practitioners and policymakers to guess what works best.

That’s why we welcome a historic investment in the National Rural Higher Education Research Center, which will evaluate “what works” for rural students and colleges. By partnering with colleges, state agencies and rural communities across the country over the next five years, it will identify and evaluate strategies that build on rural strengths to expand opportunity, increase credential completion and strengthen local economies.

The Center’s research will explore how rural students transition from high school, choose institutions, persist and enter the workforce, while recognizing that different rural regions face different challenges and opportunities. All studies are designed to suggest timely best practices that educators can bring to their own campuses.

Achieving the Dream is a Center affiliate organization. With a network of more than 300 community colleges, including a large percentage of rural and Tribal Colleges, we will create information-sharing channels between colleges, strengthen partnerships and help find practical solutions that work for students and communities.

The goal is practical, actionable research that helps institutions understand what is likely to work for their students and regions — not simply what worked somewhere else.

Meredith Archer Hatch is director of network relations for Achieving the Dream. Alyssa Ratledge is senior research associate in MDRC’s postsecondary education policy area and leads MDRC’s rural higher education work.

Contact the opinion editor at opinion@hechingerreport.org.

title: ED Clarifies How Current Students Can Access Uncapped Loans
summary:
ED Clarifies How Current Students Can Access Uncapped Loans
jessica.blake@… Mon, 08/17/2026 - 03:00 AM
Byline(s)
Jessica Blake
full_text:
Financial aid experts say the Education Department is reworking the way it determines whether existing students are eligible for uncapped loans, but a department spokesperson says the change is “not anything new.”

During a webinar last week, staffers at the Office of Federal Student Aid provided clarity about how they are calculating “expected time to credential”—or a formula that is key to determining how long certain students can remain eligible for the Grad and Parent PLUS programs under new loan limits. Instead of basing these calculations on the length of time a student is enrolled—as many financial aid experts previously understood to be the case—ED now appears to be basing them on the number of credit hours completed.

Loan experts say this is the first time they’ve heard about this change and that it’s significant because it could dramatically affect whether students who were enrolled prior to the new policy taking effect can still finance the remainder of their studies.

Congress ended Grad PLUS and put new limits on Parent PLUS last year. Those changes took effect July 1, and existing students were grandfathered in since many began their studies depending on those loans to cover college costs. Under the final regulations, they were only going to have access to the uncapped loans for up to three years or whenever they hit their program’s standard full-time length, whichever comes first. (For example, many master’s programs are expected to take two years to complete.)

Now, that formula for eligibility appears to be based on credit hours—not time.

Ellen Keast, an Education Department spokesperson, said the formula for calculating a student’s expected time to credential is not new and should not come as a surprise.

“The latest webinar and the specific question had been discussed earlier along with similar questions and answers over the past few months in the Virtual Office Hours that we have been doing with schools on implementation,” she wrote in an email to Inside Higher Ed.

The department did not, however, provide further specifics about when the updated definitions were discussed or written down. Meanwhile, financial aid administrators and loan experts noted that the department’s final rule on the new loan limits states that expected time to completion and therefore remaining eligibility for PLUS loans is based on time. They also cited an FAQ document released in May that suggests the same.

The change would apply to undergraduate and graduate students, and some experts say it could help address previous concerns that existed under the time-based model for calculating eligibility. By focusing on credit hours, they say, it would better protect part-time students from losing access to the loans before they can complete their program.

But it also raises new questions and concerns for financial aid administrators. Based on the webinar slides, it’s unclear how the change will affect students who have been taking more credits a year than the minimum required for their degree but still haven’t completed certain critical classes and whether they’ll now be cut off from PLUS loans before finishing their degree.

The timing of a shift like this is also not ideal, said Sarah Austin, a policy analyst at the National Association of Student Financial Aid Administrators. NASFAA has previously taken issue with how the Trump administration is rolling out changes to the new loan limit policies.

“It’s really about the timing of this—the fact that we’re getting a change of guidance in August when school has already started on many campuses,” Austin said. “We’re now thinking what are all the scenarios where this changes what schools have been packaging [financial aid offers based] on.”

title: Maestro College Accreditor Discloses Private Student Information
summary:
Maestro College Accreditor Discloses Private Student Information
Katherine Knott Mon, 08/17/2026 - 03:00 AM
Byline(s)
Katherine Knott
full_text:
An accreditor inadvertently shared private student information with another student, according to New America, a left-leaning think tank.

The student who received the information had complained to the Council on Occupational Education about Maestro College, an online institution that relies heavily on AI to deliver instruction. New America documented Maestro’s model in a report released last month.

Maestro, which is based in Texas, lost its accreditation in mid-July after COE determined the college’s online enrollment exceeded the accreditor’s requirement that 25 percent of full-time students attend traditional (brick-and-mortar) programs.

The latest report from New America is largely based on an interview with the student, Randi Giammona, who received the information from the accreditor, which was part of the college’s response to Giammona’s complaint. The information, which included Maestro officials’ notes about students’ personal lives, was improperly redacted, according to New America.

“Highlighting and then copying the text beneath the black box revealed the students’ identities,” New America said.

A COE spokesperson said in a statement to Inside Higher Ed that the accreditor requires institutions to redact personally identifiable information.

“COE is aware of an inadvertent disclosure of personally identifiable information in an institutional response submitted as part of an accreditation-related complaint process,” the statement said. “We take privacy seriously and are actively working to research and contain the matter, review the affected materials, and require properly redacted replacements where appropriate. Our review is ongoing, and we will communicate directly with affected parties as warranted. We are still confirming details, and we remain committed to addressing the matter responsibly and strengthening safeguards to help prevent recurrence.”

title: The Heated Discourse About Civil Discourse
summary:
The Heated Discourse About Civil Discourse
Ryan Quinn Mon, 08/17/2026 - 03:00 AM

Groups advocating for “dialogue across difference” and finding better ways to discuss and disagree about controversial topics are themselves part of a polarized debate.

Byline(s)
Ryan Quinn
full_text:
Proponents of what’s often called civil discourse education are pushing to expand this teaching—and mandate it—across entire campuses.

Earlier this month, Institute for Citizens and Scholars President Rajiv Vinnakota told state higher ed leaders that he doesn’t just want to foster civil discourse, he wants to promote “civic practice” and build “civic muscle.”

“That means giving every student opportunities to practice three essential skills: having productive conversation, discerning and using credible information, and collaborating to create solutions, even with those with whom you may disagree,” Vinnakota said.

And he went beyond calling for mere opportunities for this education. “Every student, not those who just opt in, must learn and practice these skills,” he told attendees of the State Higher Education Executive Officers Association’s Higher Ed Policy Conference in Chicago. He asked for their help, now.

“The question is no longer whether a focus on these skills belongs in higher education,” he said. “The question is how we make it central to every student’s experience, and how quickly we can move in this moment.”

But some faculty are still questioning this focus, and the motives of those who fund it. A consortium of scholars from multiple institutions called Uncivil argues that “billionaire funders and extremist politicians” are funding campus dialogue programs to “suppress organic student organizing.” It released a report in June listing which private organizations have been funding entities focused on civil discourse, “constructive dialogue” and other terms. The report also lists other groups that these donors fund, and labels those other recipients as progressive, conservative or “pro-Israel.” In doing so, the report suggests the donors’ own political allegiances.

Bethany Moreton, a Dartmouth College history professor who’s on Uncivil’s executive committee, said that what her group calls the “civility-industrial complex”—185 dialogue programs, character-education initiatives and civics centers and their funders—is perpetuating “a real slur against students” and faculty. She said this is true even if organizations such as the Institute for Citizens and Scholars have good intentions and don’t necessarily share the motivations of others who are pushing civil discourse.

“You can’t analyze the Big Civility providers without acknowledging the context, in which they’re adding fuel to the ‘patriotic education’ kinds of initiatives by giving credence to the suggestion that—somehow—American higher education is failing to help people learn how to engage with ideas,” Moreton told Inside Higher Ed.

The American Association of University Professors—a century-old professional association and now left-leaning faculty union that’s become increasingly politically involved—has raised similar objections to such criticisms of faculty. Uncivil’s executive committee includes some prominent AAUP members, but Moreton said it’s not an AAUP project.

The disagreement shows that the debate over the need for civil discourse education has itself become polarized, after universities have widely adopted these programs. The Trump administration has poured tens of millions of dollars into higher ed initiatives labeled “civil discourse.” The programs have also spread across campuses with both right- and left-leaning reputations. And advocates are currently ramping up efforts to test whether they work.

Moreton excoriated the civility-industrial complex, saying it promotes political passivity “under the color of greater engagement.” She said it doesn’t actually push people to engage with arguments and instead stokes “moral panics around the form that the argument takes” while “undermining the distinction between evidenced argument and what you might call affirmative action for bad ideas.”

“Willingly or not, they are abetting an authoritarian capture of the public sphere—if what you think you’re teaching people about appropriate political engagement is to sit quietly and listen to powerful people tell you you’re subhuman,” Moreton said.

Caroline Mehl, co-founder and executive director of the Constructive Dialogue Institute, said her group—which doesn’t specifically use the term “civil discourse”—isn’t trying to suppress student political expression. “One of the key outcomes that we care about is improving students’ comfort [with] speaking up about their political views,” she said.

She also said civil discourse groups aren’t a monolith.

“There are a group of other organizations all doing this work, but it isn’t coordinated in any kind of way right now,” she said. These organizations have started discussions about coordinating, but haven’t even decided that’s a wise move yet, she added.

And while she said her group is nonpartisan, she noted some others aren’t. “This is just a topic that people across the political spectrum care deeply about,” she said.

The Institute for Citizens and Scholars didn’t provide an interview for this article, but a representative for the group said in an email that “our organization is built explicitly to transcend partisan divides, not reinforce them.”

“C&S’s civic engagement work is backed by a deliberately broad coalition of philanthropic funders and institutions spanning the ideological spectrum, with no single funder driving our direction,” the representative wrote. He added that “meaningful civic preparation does not require ideological conformity or the suppression of disagreement. In fact, meaningful civic learning depends on helping young people navigate disagreement, complexity, and real-world challenges with both conviction and curiosity.”

A Panoply of Presidents

Vinnakota said numerous university presidents are eager to require civil discourse education campuswide.

“Campuses are moving beyond one-time events and isolated dialogue programs to make civic preparation part of the student experience, spanning everything from orientation to general education to residential life and community engagement,” he said.

He told the SHEEO conference attendees that C&S started its College Presidents for Civic Preparedness initiative back in 2021 and it now involves about 140 institution presidents reaching one million students across 34 states and Washington, D.C. He said 60 of these institutions are taking part in “Campuswide Immersion” initiatives.

C&S says participating presidents include Wesleyan University’s Michael Roth, who frequently condemns the Trump administration, and the Indiana University system’s Pamela Whitten, in whom IU Bloomington faculty voted no confidence after IU Bloomington enacted controversial restrictions on pro-Palestine expression in the wake of the October 2023 start of the Israel-Hamas war.

During the conference panel, Vinnakota spoke alongside one of those presidents: Harrison Keller of the University of North Texas. Keller said one obstacle to requiring civil discourse education is that faculty express “some fear” about what could happen to professors leading discussions about hot-button topics. Keller noted that out-of-context statements can be posted on social media and “reposted by a policymaker even before you know what’s going on.” He added that faculty wonder, “‘Would the institution have my back? I could lose my job.’”

“We had to defuse that and say, ‘We’re not asking you to do that at all, really. What we’re asking you to do is help students build this other kind of tool kit that’s actually in your area of expertise,’” Keller said. “And that really changed the whole conversation with the faculty.”

The University of North Texas, during Keller’s presidency, has repeatedly been criticized for restricting faculty rights, including ending faculty groups for minorities; removing words such as “race” and “equity” from course titles; and citing a diversity, equity and inclusion ban to stop funding conference attendance for certain journalism professors. Keller told Inside Higher Ed it’s “not optional” to follow state and federal law, though his university has been accused of overcompliance.

Dollars for Discourse

The Uncivil report, in its critique of funding for various programs, noted a $2.6 million gift from the John Templeton Foundation to C&S.

On its website, the foundation announced that, starting last fall and going through fall 2028, it’s providing $2.6 million to C&S for civil discourse work. The foundation is a massive donor to diverse organizations—its latest IRS filing online shows it gave more than $134 million in gifts in 2024 alone—many of which include colleges and universities.

The gifts often center on religion, and recipients also include conservative and libertarian groups such as the Mercatus Center and Atlas Network and free speech groups such as PEN America. An Uncivil report listed Templeton among the top 23 private funders of the civility-industrial complex.

In an email to Inside Higher Ed, the foundation said, “We are committed to curiosity and humility. We partner with a wide variety of philanthropic organizations to support the generation and exchange of ideas.” College Presidents for Civic Preparedness also lists among its supporters the Lumina Foundation, a higher ed–focused private foundation.

Mehl, of the Constructive Dialogue Institute—which was also targeted by Uncivil—said the report employs “guilt-by-association reasoning.” She said that “in general, funders support a broad range of issues, and that doesn’t mean that those issues are necessarily connected.”

She said many of the civil discourse groups, including hers, began “really in reaction to the 2016 election and the widespread divisiveness” that became apparent across the country. C&S dates back to 1945, but mostly under another name: the Woodrow Wilson National Fellowship Foundation. In November 2020—just after Joe Biden was elected president—it announced its current name, saying in a news release that Wilson’s “racist policies and beliefs are fundamentally incompatible with the organization’s values and work.” (Wilson, a Princeton University and U.S. president, supported segregation and famously showed The Birth of a Nation in the White House.)

Universities sought to ramp up their civil discourse education efforts after pro-Palestinian student protests rippled across campuses. Those demonstrations and encampments attracted condemnation from some Jewish and pro-Israel groups, and from politicians. Moreton, of Uncivil, argues that traditional conservative funders of civil discourse programs have been joined by pro-Israel groups.

“Pathologizing pro-Palestinian student advocacy—the utility of that move to the authoritarian and ethnonationalist forces in the United States should be obvious,” Moreton said. “It is a shared ethnonationalist project to pathologize protest, and it will have consequences.”

Whatever the political persuasion of the civil discourse programs are now, or in the future, students should brace for more of them.

“We’ll know we’re doing it right if, by the time students get to junior year … they’re like, ‘If I have to do one more collaborative problem-solving activity, I’m going to vomit,’” Keller said. “Then I think we’ll just be right about at the sweet spot.”

title: How LGBTQ+ Higher Ed Leaders Are Navigating the Political Moment
summary:
How LGBTQ+ Higher Ed Leaders Are Navigating the Political Moment
Sara Weissman Mon, 08/17/2026 - 03:00 AM

A group for LGBTQ+ higher ed administrators has been hit hard by an increasingly hostile policy landscape. But members are working to support each other.

Byline(s)
Sara Weissman
full_text:
When the group LGBTQ Leaders in Higher Education started taking shape in the 2000s, it consisted of a handful of out-of-the-closet presidents who gathered informally to swap guidance. More than a decade later, it’s a thriving professional development organization for upward of 100 presidents, chancellors, deans, department heads, directors and other administrators. But it’s been a hard year for the group and its members as political headwinds batter both higher ed and LGBTQ+ communities.

State and federal bans on diversity, equity and inclusion initiatives have chilled some campus programming for LGBTQ+ staff and students. The Trump administration targeted universities for welcoming trans athletes and students. Federal agencies axed grants related to LGBTQ+ subjects, and an executive order sought to establish “two sexes.” In response to government restrictions, some universities deleted messages for Pride Month and dropped out of events. Others eliminated LGBTQ+ affinity housing and graduation celebrations.

Jim Berg, executive director of LGBTQ Leaders in Higher Education (which was known as LGBTQ Presidents in Higher Education until 2023), said the nonprofit has been affected by the upheaval while also working to support members through it.

Some LGBTQ+ leaders’ gender expressions don’t match their government-issued IDs, making them hesitant to travel for the group’s annual leadership institutes, Berg said. Some colleges and universities are no longer willing—or question if they’re legally allowed—to pay for administrators to attend events or purchase institutional memberships. The organization, which subsists on memberships, saw individual members rise but institutional memberships drop off by a whopping 30 percent in 2025. The financial hit forced the group to reconfigure its budget and rely more on fundraising.

“It was an immediate impact after this administration took over,” Berg said.

Susan Henking, president of Wells College and a board member for LGBTQ Leaders in Higher Education, said she worries about LGBTQ+ presidents and leaders who want to be open about their identities and speak out on politics but fear ramifications for their institutions. She said colleagues in states like Florida and Texas, where state lawmakers have targeted diversity work, are “trying to get out.” Meanwhile, “it’s a low-level burnout phenomenon constantly for everyone.”

She emphasized that higher ed leaders are focused on how the political moment is affecting students, but they’re struggling, too.

“The political situation we’re living in, in my view, is catastrophically bad for higher education generally and catastrophically bad for LGBTQ people,” Henking said. “It feels like it’s pushing people back into a closet, forcing them to choose between their personal lives and the lives of their institutions … It’s not just chilling; it’s frightening.”

She said campuses benefit when leaders feel they can be their full selves.

“There’s some price to pay for living with your heart on your sleeve a little bit,” she said, “but there are some advantages to it, too. I think we really need to help leaders be persons as well as leaders, and I think that actually also helps students and faculty and staff.”

Bolstering Supports

LGBTQ Leaders in Higher Education hopes to serve as a source of community and belonging for LGBTQ+ administrators as they navigate these heightened challenges.

Kristin Esterberg, chancellor of the University of Washington, Bothell, and a board member of the LGBTQ leadership group, said administrators’ experiences range widely depending on what types of institution they lead and where they’re located, so the resources they’re seeking out vary.

Some needs are evergreen. For example, members have often turned to the organization for professional advice—especially up-and-coming administrators looking to throw their hats into the ring for a presidency or chancellorship. Webinars with search consultants help them prepare, as does the organization’s mentorship program.

“The search process is always a challenge for LGBTQ leaders,” especially trans and nonbinary candidates, said Esterberg, former president of the organization’s board. Members often come in with questions about how forthcoming to be about their identities or what role their spouse or partner might play on campus. “Members who are looking for a leadership position have to think about, what are they navigating? When I was engaged in my first presidential search, I thought a lot about are there places I couldn’t bring my family, or wouldn’t want to bring my family?”

The group has also introduced new programming to meet the moment.

This year, the organization emphasized personal wellness at its in-person leadership institute, Berg said. It also introduced more virtual programming focused on community building, including regional webinars for administrators in parts of the country that might be more hostile to LGBTQ+ communities.

“It’s often the case that an out administrator might be the only out person on their campus, or the only out person in leadership at their institution,” he said. “We can help them to find a provost or somebody who has a similar job that they do but in a neighboring state to try to help them to build community that way.”

Daniel López, president of Harold Washington College in Chicago, said LGBTQ Leaders in Higher Education has been “instrumental” to him for guidance as anti-DEI policies have proliferated in recent years. He’s been involved with the organization for over a decade and joined the board about six years ago.

He finds the federal policy landscape to be among the most challenging he’s experienced in his 30-plus years in higher education. Even in a blue state like Illinois, he said it’s jarring to have watched the legalization of domestic partnerships and then gay marriage, only to find LGBTQ+ rights “under attack” later in his career.

“The biggest challenge is trying to continue to do our work when we get specific directives from this administration about DEI,” López said, “and all the things that we have put in place to protect, to support our LGBT community, that’s all being questioned.”

But he described his colleagues as a support system. For example, he’s called up other leaders to brainstorm the best ways to check in with and offer support to trans students, faculty and staff members under the Trump administration.

At least “we’re navigating through this together,” López said.

Moving Forward

Berg emphasized that the landscape for LGBTQ+ people in higher ed is not all doom and gloom.

He pointed out that even in this political moment, LGBTQ+ leaders are assuming new presidencies. A board member, Luca E. Lewis, became the first out trans college or university president when he took the helm at Ventura College this year.

Despite challenges, “we’ve had some good wins,” Berg said. “One thing that we’re trying to provide is hope. We’re in it for the long haul. We’re not going to disappear tomorrow.”

He wants LGBTQ+ higher ed leaders to know that “there’s an organization who cares about them … that they can find community if they’re not finding it on their campus or that they can learn from us and build community where they are,” he added. “If we can all work together, we can weather this current condition.”

Esterberg also stressed that the moment and its challenges will pass, and part of the organization’s job is to help members get through it. As a sociologist who researched LGBTQ+ movements during the McCarthy era, she takes the “long view.”

“All movements have periods of upswing and then abeyance,” she said, “and so maybe we’re in a period of abeyance right now. And the importance of organizations is to continue to build base, to continue to build strategy and to keep moving forward.”

title: Awaiting answers: On the student protests in Jharkhand
summary: Student agitations in Ranchi reveal angst over flawed exam processes
full_text:
When the route up the economic ladder in society is limited to an ever-narrowing range of options in the public sector, and the process of gaining entry through entrance examinations becomes tainted, angst and agitation are the results. This is why students in Jharkhand, loosely organised into two platforms — the Jharkhand Public Service Commission (JPSC)-Jharkhand Staff Selection Commission (JSSC) Abhyarthi Nyay Manch and the JPSC-JSSC Reform Manch — have been protesting in Ranchi for over three weeks. The trigger was the July 2 result of the JPSC’s 14th Combined Civil Services preliminary examination, which shortlisted 2,204 candidates from about 3.5 lakh aspirants for 103 posts. Aspirants pointed to undisclosed category-wise cut-offs, oddities in the merit list, a widely circulated OMR sheet on which an ostensibly successful candidate had attempted fewer than half the questions, and the fact that the conducting agency had been blacklisted in May 2025. The two platforms differ in their political leanings and have sought to negotiate separately with the government, but both want the cancellation of the disputed JPSC and JSSC exams, a CBI investigation and prosecution of officials, besides the reconstitution of commissions and a predictable examination calendar. The Jharkhand Mukti Morcha-led coalition government has responded with CID raids, arrests, resignations in the JPSC, and a cabinet committee. On Monday it went further, announcing the cancellation of all examinations conducted since 2014 by the outsourced agency, TSR Data Processing, which might help assuage the agitating students but could leave those who cleared the examinations fairly in the lurch.

The rot in the exam system is deep-rooted. Since the State’s formation in 2000, results have frequently been delayed and cycles have been bunched up many times. In a recent JSSC exam, an SIT reported no organised leak despite CID reports that described money changing hands for pre-examination access. These have eroded students’ trust in the government; hence the demand for a CBI probe. The 2003 and 2005 exams were subject to CBI scrutiny but the cases are still pending. Yet, the Hemant Soren-led government should concede this politically unpalatable demand, along with other steps, including a fixed exam calendar, and fair and transparent marking with clear cut-offs and time-bound results. Jharkhand is one of India’s poorest States, and its mineral wealth has not led to sufficient employment. With youth forced to rely on monsoon-dependent agriculture and allied activities, a government job offers a steady option. Aspirants spend years in coaching centres and libraries in pursuit of this. The youth deserve not only a fair recruitment system but also a government that diversifies their options for gainful employment.

The post Conquer the First-Day Teaching Anxiety: Tips for a Strong First Impression appeared first on Faculty Focus | Higher Ed Teaching & Learning.
full_text:
The first day of college teaching could be the most stressful moment ever in the teaching history of novice faculty members. Generally, the first day of teaching is intimidating for both faculty and students. According to Aydin (2021), it is common to experience anxiety on the first day of teaching, especially among newly experienced faculty members.

Anxiety emotions are mixtures of conceptualizations such as cognitive, physiological, motivational, and expressive components. In addition to the tendency for perfectionism (Aydin, 2021). According to Gaines et al. (2025), the stressful emotions teachers face on the first day of teaching are strongly related to cognitive appraisal theory. The theory explains that emotions result from individual interpretations and appraisals of events and situations. These emotions reflect on individuals’ actions and thoughts (Gaines et al., 2025).

Novice teachers most commonly experience these specific stressful emotions that might lead to experiencing anxiety on the first day of teaching.

Another reason for the first-day teaching anxiety could lie in imposter syndrome. According to Shekhawat & Kumar (2023), Imposter syndrome is a psychological status characterized by persistent feelings of inadequacy, self-doubt, and not being worthy in that place, despite evidence of competence and accomplishments (Shekhawat & Kumar, 2023).

It is the negative inner self-thoughts that doubt self-credibility and qualifications. It has been reported that 79% of new teachers experience imposter syndrome and societal expectations (Shekhawat & Kumar, 2023). Social expectations lead to fear of facing students’ criticism and judgment. The problem is that these feelings are real and powerful, to the point that they could adversely affect students’ first-day impression.

Therefore, educators should understand the nature of this anxiety, its roots, and how to overcome it. Otherwise, these thoughts would undermine teachers’ self-esteem and self-confidence.

Let Go of Perfection and Focus on Connection

Setting perfection as a main goal in a new teaching experience is not recommended. According to Jossberger et al. (2025), the high level of teaching performance expertise is not rooted in unique, inherent traits; rather, it is a set of skills that grow over time. It is recommended to not expect perfection in the first round of teaching. Instead, focus on building rapport with your students (Haller, 2025).

Building an effective, inclusive classroom community starts on the first day of school by introducing yourself, your name, and how you would like to be called. Students need to feel your enthusiasm for teaching your course as you introduce yourself. Talk about your credibility, activities, hobbies, and favorite sport.

In addition, the first day of teaching is the day to start. Learning the students’ names. Practicing memorizing students’ names is a key to building a good rapport with them (Buddle, 2014). Use whatever tricks you can to memorize your student’s name. Even if an educator could not get it completely right in the first week, students would appreciate your potential and caring.

Consider How Your First Impressions Begins Before Class

In preparing for the first day of teaching, new faculty may consider their outfit selection. Of course, formal attire would generally be the first choice, but consider that there is a strong connection between the instructor’s first-day outfit and students’ perceptions on the first day of school (Oliver et al., 2021) Instructors who wear a highly formal outfit on the first day of teaching are perceived by students as a sign of competence, credibility, and strictness. However, it also conveys a message of decreased warmth, enthusiasm, friendliness, and sympathy (Oliver et al., 2021). Therefore, depending on your preferences, be mindful that your first day outfit also plays a role in students’ expectations and perceptions. If you choose the informal academic outfit, just be careful to keep your teaching tone formal with your students (Oliver et al., 2021).

Prepare Your Classroom Before Students Arrive

I would recommend becoming familiar with classroom arrangements and settings before students enter the classroom, check the technology tools, set your PowerPoint slides ready to launch, and communicate with other colleagues for support in case of hiccups (First Day of Class | Teaching + Learning Lab, 2025).

Use Icebreakers to Build Classroom Community

Be minful of the power of icebreaker activities in reducing anxiety on the first day of school for both students and instructors. The incorporation of icebreaker activities would help foster a class environment conducive to communication (Great Start and High Note Ending – Lansing Community College, 2026). Additionally, it would reflect on the first-day impression as students recognize that their instructor cares about getting to know them. Finally, the use of icebreaker activities would facilitate the formation of friendships among classmates.

There are a variety of icebreaker activities that instructors could use on the first day of class. For example, assigning students into groups of two or four and having them introduce themselves to one another. Alternatively, it could be more creative, like the” Five Fingers” activity, where each student shares with the class more about themselves using their five fingers theme as follows (Great Start and High Note Ending – Lansing Community College, 2026):

Thumb for naming something they are good at.

Pointer for stating a career goal

Middle finger to tell something that makes you happy (could be a favorite snack)

Ring finger to name someone or something special

Pinky to name something that will have your classmate remember you

Make the Syllabus Part of the First-Day Experience

According to (Meyers & Smith, 2024), students’ impression of the first day teaching is strongly related to their interests in the course (Meyers & Smith, 2024). Therefore, on the first day, prepare to use the session time wisely and introduce the course syllabus to students to explain what you expect from students according to syllabus policies. The more time the instructor spends explaining the course objectives, the greater the students’ satisfaction with the first day (Meyers & Smith, 2024). Ensure that each student reads the syllabus and understands the grading system, attendance rules, and the emphasis on class participation. You may implement activities such as a syllable scavenger hunt or low-stakes quizzes to confirm students’ knowledge of the course syllabus (Meyers & Smith, 2024).

Your First Day Is a Starting Point, Not a Finish Line

Stressful thoughts during the preparation for the first day of teaching are common among faculty members, as it is normal to have these doubts and worries (Buddle, 2014). In the meantime, as a novice instructor, you need to demonstrate self confidence in front of your students, especially on the first day of teaching. Seeking support from other colleagues and advisors is recommended. I would also recommend attending the professional teaching workshops that provide a venue for exchanging experiences and expertise to overcome first-day teaching anxiety.

She is an active member of the California Dental Association (CDA) and the American Dental Hygienists’ Association (ADHA). She is dedicated to teaching and passionate about knowledge dissemination.

title: UF and Neutrality
summary:
UF and its Neutrality Policy

On September 10, I posted a comment on Facebook I now regret that was critical of Charlie Kirk and President Trump. Like much that appears on social media it was unnecessarily sharply worded but well within what courts regard as protected speech. Nevertheless, the University did not response. In fact, a document search revealed no communication with the University about this comment for several days until September 18 when I was cyber-bullied at the behest, I am told but do not know, of Scott Presler.  Late that same night, at  10:48 P.M.,  I received a terse unsigned email from the self-proclaimed “neutral” UF administration, indicating that my emeritus status had been revoked.  The notice was careful not to say why because that would raise pesky First Amendment issues. In their own version of cyber-bullying, this news was made public by the University on social media  for all to see and reported by the Alligator and the Gainesville Sun the next morning. I was given no opportunity to respond.

I have repeatedly tried to engage President Landry and other University officials in a discussion of other less callous actions that were actually neutral. There was no response at all,  no doubt by the order of the University’s massive team of attorneys. For example, I could have been informed privately of my punishment. More simply and logically the University could have posted on social media “Professor Harrison has not been employed by the University for five years and his views do not reflect those of the University.” That would be an example of neutrality, a policy to which the President pledged to adhere but obviously did not.

There are lessons here regarding the 1st Amendment and its, like my own, demotion in the view of the University. This is also a lesson for a University president of only 18 days about snap decisions and who he should rely on for advice in the future. But putting all that aside (and it’s a lot) what we learned is the University is a vindictive place, plays to a specific audience,  and it is quick to attach a high tech version of the letter A to those who dissent. 

PS: President Landry in a kindly written note restored my emeritus status during his last day or two of his role as Interim President. My hunch is that this did not sit well with the interim provost but I cannot be sure

Jeffrey L. Harrison

title: A People’s (with apologies to Zinn) Ranking of Law Schools
summary:
Actually I cannot give you the rankings other than to say it would look nothing like the elitist, manipulation-prone ranking of US News. These are, however, the factors that would go into a true ranking of  law schools.

1. Percentage of class with less than 160 LSAT score. Why? Dolts can and do teach students with over  160 scores. That does not take any real teaching ability. Those students will get it. Teaching them is like teaching native German speakers how to speak German. 

2. Percentage of students with below 160 who pass the bar. This is the real measure of teaching effectiveness because those students may actually need teaching expertise.

3. Number of citations by courts of scholarly works per faculty member. In a prior study a colleague and I demonstrated that citations by other law professors are irrelevant. They generally do not rely on anything but factual assertions and rarely engage the thoughts of the works they cite. Let's face it. If courts do not cite your work, you are wasting your time and writing for a very small and irrelevant audience.

4. Percentage of students who are first in family college graduates. These people are likely to have a different perspective on virtually everything than the entitled ones, Want to have lively class discussion? Admit these people.

5. Percentage of faculty who did not graduate from top 15 law schools. Quite honestly, in 42 years of law teaching, the most poorly educated and laziest people I have met came from elite undergraduate and law schools. I could name names but that would take 5 blogs. They are the grade grubbers who focused on one thing -- what is on the test. Want some diversity away from the same old name dropping dolts, expand your hiring horizons. 

6. Number of African-American faculty. I know there are all kinds of minorities these days but none come close to this group in terms of having been kicked around, discriminated against, and pushed aside. Want you students to be more well rounded, better able to interact with diverse clients, then hire these people.

7. Percentage of financial aid distributed on the basis of need. Yes, this is different from the School were I taught which engaged in a bidding war for high LSATs.

8. Percentage of graduates who opt for public interest employment. Hopefully, 3 years of exposure to law school and the way law is consistently applied to favor the haves would encourage some students to, at least for some period of time, do the right thing.
